The morning light hit the windowsill at exactly 6:47, and I realized I'd been holding my breath. Not for any reason. Just one of those things the body does when the mind wanders too far from its machinery. I exhaled, watched the dust motes scatter and regather in the golden shaft, these tiny constellations that exist only in the angle between a sun and a room.

I've been thinking about angles lately. The way a conversation turns just slightly and suddenly you're somewhere else entirely, looking back at where you stood wondering how you got here. The angle of my father's jaw in photographs from before I was born, when he was still someone I don't recognize, a young man with hope that hadn't yet been tested for tensile strength. The angle of my cat's ears when she hears something I can't, that precise forty-five degree alertness that says *the world is larger than your senses permit*.

My grandmother kept a jar of buttons on her dresser. Not organized. Not color-coded. Just hundreds of buttons accumulated across decades, from garments that had long since dissolved into rags, then memory, then nothing. I would run my fingers through them as a child, this cascading chatter of plastic and shell and metal, and feel something I couldn't name. It was the sound of time being patient. The sound of things waiting for purposes they might never regain. I have my own jar now, though I don't sew. I add to it slowly. A button from a coat I loved that tore beyond repair. One I found in a parking lot, still threaded with a fragment of blue fabric, someone's loss that became my curation. I shake it sometimes and listen, and I'm eight again, and she's alive, and the buttons are still talking.

There's a theory I read somewhere that every cell in your body replaces itself over seven years, which means I'm now composed of materials that never touched her kitchen table, never smelled her lilac soap, never knew the particular creak of her third stair. But the buttons remain. The buttons outlast. I hold one between my fingers and think: *this was fastened against wind, against cold, against exposure*. The original function persists in the form. We are all, maybe, original functions persisting in altered forms.

I walked through the old neighborhood last October. The elm on Crescent Street had been removed, the one we carved nothing into because we were superstitious about permanence, because we wanted to believe we could return unchanged. The stump was still there, wider than my outstretched arms could measure, rings upon rings upon rings. I counted back to one that must have been 1987, the year I was born, the year the tree was already substantial, already doing its slow work of upward and outward while I was just beginning my own. We grew together without knowing each other. We shared groundwater, air, the particular slant of afternoon light in that latitude. Now I continue, and it doesn't, except in the way that cut trees continue in the houses they become, the paper they become, the carbon they release back to the cycle we pretend we're outside of.

I sat on the curb for a while. A man walked past with a dog that looked like it had been assembled from spare parts—one ear up, one down, coat of no particular color. The dog looked at me with what I can only call recognition, though we'd never met. Maybe it was the sitting. The being still in a world that moves. The dog would not be hurried, and the man stopped, and we talked about nothing, and then they continued around the corner, and I never learned either of their names, and this is the way most encounters go, these brief intersections that don't accumulate into narrative but somehow still matter, still deposit something in the sediment of who we become.

I used to want everything to mean something. The career, the trajectory, the coherent story you tell at reunions. Now I suspect meaning is more like the buttons—accumulated, disordered, occasionally useful but mostly just present, witnesses to the fact that you were here, you fastened things against the wind, you came undone and were refastened or not, you persisted in your form.

The word *persists* keeps coming. I think it's because I'm tired of the language of transformation, the imperative to become, to optimize, to shed your skin like it's a moral failing to keep any of it. I want to honor the skin. The callus on my right middle finger from holding pens wrong since I was six. The scar on my knee from a bicycle I don't remember the color of. The way I still startle at loud noises, still want to be chosen first in games I no longer play, still wake sometimes at 3 AM with the specific dread that I have forgotten something important and it's too late to recover it.

What if nothing is recovered? What if everything important is precisely what we don't retain, what leaks through the fingers of attention, what we weren't even aware we were learning? My grandmother never taught me to sew. I don't know her recipe for the cookies I remember tasting. But I know the sound of buttons, the patience of her hands, the way she said my name like it was a complete sentence. I know that love can be a jar of objects without order, waiting.

The light has moved. It's 7:23 now, and the dust motes have shifted to a different quadrant of the room, and I'm breathing regularly, and somewhere a dog is walking with a person who doesn't hurry it, and a tree is either growing or it isn't, and the cells of my body are quietly replacing themselves while I sit here, becoming someone who will still shake a jar of buttons and hear her, still sit on curbs and talk to strangers, still hold my breath for no reason and then release it, release it, release it.
